name: Vesper Republic
summary: A young republic that came out of a fallen monarchy and three failed attempts at a constitution, and now runs on public argument, political clubs and the belief that an institution isn't legitimate just because it's old.
government: A republic under the Charter of Citizens: a representative legislature, elected executive bodies, independent courts and strong municipalities.
knownFor: Political clubs and posters, iron-and-glass cities, early (sometimes too early) technology, and arguing in public.
gateAttitude: Vesper strongly resists monopolies over magical knowledge.
beliefs:
Vesper follows the **Sacred Flame**, its branch of the **Faith of the First Light** (Aurelia's branch is the Crowned Sun). Both start from Light appearing in darkness and making the world knowable; where Aurelia reads that Light as the proper order of things, Vesper reads it as something given to each person. Every thinking person carries a **Spark** of it, so no king, priest or university holds all of the truth. The best-known phrase, *one flame lights another and loses nothing*, is used wherever knowledge or help is passed on, and it's why Vesperian arguments about restricted Gate research are theological as well as political.

The First Light itself is the **Crownless God**, the same Light Aurelians call Aurelion, but one that refuses every throne. The best-loved Lantern-Bearers are **Vespara**, Bearer of Dawn, whose teaching is three words long (*It could be otherwise*); **Talien**, Maker of Questions, patron of scholars and children, whose tradition says that asking a question isn't disobedience; and **Marenne** of the Open Door, patron of shelter and mutual aid, who keeps the faith from becoming purely individual. The old warning tale is the **Ashen King**, who put out every flame in his realm but his own, until a wind came: *a thousand flames are safer than one.* Aurelia tells the same old story as the Shadow Behind the Crown, with a different lesson, and the original is lost.

The Revolution split the clergy, and modern Vesper has committed believers, secular citizens and atheists side by side. Plenty of people who'd never call themselves religious still light a lamp before starting something important. At a funeral, a flame is lit for the dead and passed into the mourners' candles; the Spark is said to return to the First Flame and to continue through the people the dead changed. The Gates mostly caused fascination, along with two open questions: the **Infinite Flame** (do thinking beings beyond the Gates carry Sparks of their own?) and the **Stolen Flame** (does taking a Core take something essential from another world?).

Older belief survives only in fragments: festival masks, a procession with an odd route, children's stories that might once have been prayers, faces carved over doorways. Ask what a custom means and you'll hear *"It's not religious. My grandmother did it."* Anyone in Endros selling the names of the old Vesperian gods is selling something, usually a book.
history:
Before the Revolution the country was the **Kingdom of Solenne**, ruled by the House of Solenne; the name *Vesper* belongs to the Republic. It wasn't a backward country. It had industry, shipbuilding and a rising urban middle class, and it was modernising faster than its politics: power stayed with the monarchy and a narrow elite while everyone else gained a stake in the country and no say in it.

The crisis that ended it is remembered as the **Year of Ash**: bad harvests, bank failures, rising taxes and demonstrations, until the monarchy's survival depended on force. Then soldiers ordered to fire on a crowd **refused**. The refusal didn't bring the monarchy down on its own, but it showed that royal authority no longer commanded obedience, and the King eventually fled. Every political tradition in Vesper claims those soldiers, and nearly every Vesperian accepts what they stand for: *obedience doesn't erase your own moral responsibility.* Which regiment it was, and in which square, the Archive can't settle.

What followed was messy. The **Three Republics** were three attempts at a lasting order: the first collapsed, the second was overthrown by moderates and officers, the third came close to dictatorship. Today's Republic rests on the **Charter of Citizens**, which has been amended many times, and Vesperians count that as a sign of health. Citizenship means taking part: voting, debating, jury service, joining things. Someone who never takes part is still a citizen, just not one people admire.

Vesper is sometimes called the **Republic of Clubs**: political clubs, unions, scientific societies, student groups, newspapers, cafés and neighbourhood committees, and one person can belong to five of them. Vesperians tie new technology to the idea that society can change too, so the Republic adopts things early. An Aurelian asks *"Has this been properly tested?"* and a Vesperian answers *"How else are we meant to test it?"* Officially it respects other states' sovereignty; unofficially Vesperian groups have long sent foreign reformers pamphlets, money, volunteers and printing presses. Whether to export revolution is an argument that has never been settled, and asking about it at dinner is a good way to lose the evening.

**The Gates.** The instinct fits on a poster, and is on many: **No Crown Owns the Impossible**. Vesper pushes for open publication and against monopolies on Gate knowledge. That has produced real progress, and also the **Open Archive Incident**: **Dr. Celeste Marin** leaked restricted research on an artifact from [[white-expanse|the White Expanse]] to five universities. Seventeen institutions ran experiments on it, two were destroyed, significant discoveries were made, and the research was banned in three countries. Marin later joined the Academy under circumstances still not fully public. Her supporters and her critics agree on what happened. They disagree on what it proves.
visualSummary:
Vesper looks like a country that believes the future will be better and intends to argue about the details. The palette is the brightest of the great powers: **red, cream, blue, gold and green**. The emblem is a torch whose flame rises from a sunburst, framed by laurel and a ring of gear teeth. Cities are iron and glass: arcades, boulevards, tram lines, great stations and cafés, with every wall covered in posters for meetings, strikes, lectures, attacks on politicians and soap. (For players: think Belle Époque and Art Nouveau.)

Dress leaves room for personal expression, and Vesperians use it: fitted long coats, colourful waistcoats, and above all the **scarf**, whose colour can say a lot about your politics, plus pins and badges for every society, union and cause you belong to. Even a uniform rarely stays uniform. Machines are meant to be beautiful too, in enamel and curving ironwork, because something people have to live next to should be pleasant to live next to.

The admired Vesperian is engaged and curious, and willing to challenge and to explain why. Foreigners decide Vesper is chaotic, that everyone is a revolutionary and that nothing ever gets decided. The arguments are loud, but the trams run, the courts sit and the Charter is amended by procedure, not riots. Most Vesperians were just raised to think asking *why* is a citizen's job, and they expect you to have an answer.
materials: Painted iron, glass, copper, brass, enamel and printed paper

relations.text: Ideological rivals: scrupulously formal diplomacy over real hostility, and the same faith read differently.
Its small neighbour: shared academic culture, constant argument over restricted research.
Admires Vardic craft and independence; the Vards wish the politics came with fewer speeches.
Economically entangled, philosophically argumentative: Vesper needs Kharadi credit and attacks concentrated wealth.
Admires its scholarship, criticises its hierarchy; Tianzhao still calls Vesper 'Solenne'.

extraRule: Once per session, establish that your sponsor or one of its affiliated societies provided a reasonable, useful contact relevant to the problem: information, an introduction or limited assistance. The contact can't solve the main problem for you.
